newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business stories.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business stories.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Wednesday:

* Two investors have separately acquired large interests in Dow Jones & Co. They are James Cramer, the manager of a private investment fund who said he holds slightly more than one million shares, and Michael Price, who owns 4.5 million shares.
* Analysts say ITT Corp will fight Hilton Hotels' hostile $6.5 billion bid.
* General Motors said its 1996 profits fell because of strike-related losses that cut its after-tax income by $1.2 billion.

* International Business Machines announced its first stock split since 1979. The ensuing $5 rise in IBM shares helped lift the market up by 100 points early in the day, but the Dow industrials gave up the gains and closed at 6,656.08.
* The 30-year Treasury yield fell to 6.92 percent from 6.94 percent.
* Mutual fund managers are keeping cash cushions at their lowest levels in 20 years.
* The Securities and Exchange Commission adopted rules that will force American companies to provide more information about their derivative securities to investors.
* RJR Nabisco said fourth quarter earnings improved, in part from revenues in its international tobacco operations and its food business.
* MCI and GTE reported higher earnings that met analysts' estimates.
* Pharmaceutical companies Merck, American Home Products and Warner-Lambert reported fourth-quarter earnings that exceeded analysts' expectations.
* UAL Corp said its profits rose from more full-fare business passengers in the U.S. and improving sales overseas.
* The National Association of Securities Dealers names Frank Zarb president.
* A Clinton administration official tells computer industry officials that they should support the proposed global standard on data encryption.
* Experts say recent investment swindles in Albania that have cost people hundreds of millions of dollars fit into a pattern found in other former communist countries in Europe.
* The latest government Employment Cost Index figures indicate that wages have not increased at a pace that would raise the rate of inflation.
* The Treasury will begin auctioning $7 billion in 10-year inflation-indexed bonds that will likely pay an interest rate of a little more than 3.5 percent.
